gaps.discriminates: Endometritis vs. pyelonephritis vs. pneumonia — uterine tenderness strongly supports endometritis; its absence would significantly reduce likelihood.
Endometritis vs. pyelonephritis — positive urine culture with >10^5 CFU/mL and pyuria would favor pyelonephritis; negative studies would weaken it substantially.
Endometritis vs. pneumonia — presence of infiltrate or effusion would confirm pneumonia; absence makes it less likely but not excluded if early or subtle.

- No chills, night sweats, or purulent discharge — consistent with *early*, not fulminant, endometritis.  
- Dyspnea is mild — plausibly reflects systemic inflammatory response (e.g., tachypnea as part of SIRS) rather than primary pulmonary disease.  

[GAPS]  
- Uterine size, consistency, and tenderness on bimanual exam — critical to assess for endometritis but not performed or reported.  
- Quantitative lochia assessment (volume, duration, clots) — subjective denial of “abnormal” discharge is insufficient; scant or serosanguineous lochia can still accompany infection.  
- Urinalysis and urine culture results — needed to definitively exclude UTI/pyelonephritis.  
- CRP and procalcitonin — elevated CRP is nearly universal in endometritis; procalcitonin helps distinguish bacterial infection from non-infectious inflammation.  
- Pelvic ultrasound findings — to rule out retained products of conception or fluid collections supporting endometritis.  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Postpartum endometritis
